summary: The mechanism and its rationale hold. Zero-list really is insufficient as the bound (a backward walk and a stat probe both pass it at one request per checkpoint), the discriminator chosen -- total across all verbs, and StoreCounts.total() does include stats -- is the right one, the stat-before-get reason is TRUE as stated (BinStore.java:32-46 documents IOException as 'the store is unreachable' and offers no not-found type on get), the lease-as-pointer-home hazard is REAL rather than invented (a second writer on the putIfMatch object whose empty result is the fencing signal M4.17 made load-bearing), the body-not-sequence choice is proportionate (one GET instead of two, no second wire format), and the two-PUT cost is per trigger per chain and scales with nothing non-negotiable 6 forbids. The failure path converges as claimed, by code reading. What the diff does NOT have is a test for the property that IS the mechanism. Measured in my own tree: (1) put -> putIfAbsent on the pointer leaves the ENTIRE build green -- so 'overwritten on every successful checkpoint' is unasserted, and the mutant freezes discovery at the first checkpoint of the epoch for ever; (2) new LogKeys(prefix, epoch) -> new LogKeys(prefix, 1L) in newestCheckpoint leaves all 282 sequencer tests green -- the epoch parameter is unconstrained, the mirror of the hardcoded-epoch mutant M4.8b2's review caught on the writer side. Both are silent in production and both feed M4.9. Three minors recorded, not blocking.

findings.summary: The defining property of ADR-0034 -- that the pointer is OVERWRITTEN on every successful checkpoint, which is the only reason it names the NEWEST one -- is asserted by nothing. MEASURED: changing `store.put(keys.latestCheckpointKey(), ...)` to `store.putIfAbsent(...)` leaves the WHOLE build green (`./gradlew test`, 34s, BUILD SUCCESSFUL). Every discovery test in CheckpointDiscoveryTest seeds the pointer by hand (seeded(int) writes it directly), and the one test that exercises the writer, theWriterMAINTAINSThePointerSoDiscoveryFindsWhatItJustWrote, drives exactly ONE checkpoint -- which putIfAbsent satisfies perfectly. Nothing anywhere writes two checkpoints and asserts the pointer moved. The comment at the site ('`put`, not `putIfAbsent`: this key is MEANT to be overwritten') is therefore an unpinned rationale of exactly the shape M4.8b2's row catalogues four times.
findings.failure_scenario: A later refactor unifies the two checkpoint writes on putIfAbsent -- an attractive change, since the seq-keyed write beside it uses putIfAbsent and the comment justifying the difference is one line. The tree stays green. In production the pointer is written once, at the first checkpoint of each epoch, and never again. Discovery keeps returning that first checkpoint, whose sequence recedes indefinitely, and M4.9's 'newest checkpoint plus at most K deltas' silently becomes a replay of the entire term -- the unbounded recovery checkpoints exist to remove, with nothing thrown and nothing logged. The same hole admits any mutation that leaves the pointer stale (writing the pointer before `body` is recomputed, hoisting it out of the loop of triggers, caching the first body).
findings.remedy: Drive TWO triggers through CheckpointWriter and assert ChainReplay.newestCheckpoint returns the SECOND sequence -- the assertion that must be relative to the two writes, not to a constant. Measured: that kills the putIfAbsent mutant.

findings.summary: newestCheckpoint's `epoch` parameter is unconstrained by any test. MEASURED: replacing `new LogKeys(prefix, epoch).latestCheckpointKey()` with `new LogKeys(prefix, 1L).latestCheckpointKey()` leaves all 282 sequencer tests green (`--rerun-tasks`, BUILD SUCCESSFUL); every case in CheckpointDiscoveryTest uses epoch 1. This is the reader-side mirror of the mutant M4.8b2's own review caught on the writer ('a HARDCODED epoch in the key survived everything, which after a failover puts checkpoints under the sealed ancestor's prefix where M4.8b1's own filter makes the loss SILENT'), reintroduced one commit later. A positive control confirms the harness is sensitive to edits in this method: returning empty unconditionally fails 3 tests.
findings.failure_scenario: The parameter is the only thing that selects WHICH term's checkpoint is returned, and this is the method M4.9 will call at takeover, when the interesting epoch is an ancestor's rather than the caller's own. Any edit that resolves the wrong epoch -- a hardcoded value, an off-by-one against the ancestry hop, reusing ChainReplay's ownEpoch where the hop's epoch was meant -- returns a checkpoint from a different term. Its per-stream nextOffsets then become the recovering leader's resume point, so offsets are re-assigned from a stale or foreign watermark: I2, and silent, because M4.8b1's key filter means nothing under the wrong prefix ever fails to decode.
findings.remedy: One case with the pointer written at an epoch >= 2 (assert it is found), and one where epoch N has a pointer and N+1 does not (assert N+1 is empty). Both are cheap against the existing seeded() fixture.

findings.summary: The new PUT's RATE is outside every rate assertion this milestone built. RecordingBinStore's checkpointKeys(), checkpointBodies() and lastCheckpointBody() all filter on `endsWith(".ckpt")`, and `ckpt/LATEST` does not match, so the pointer is invisible to the assertions M4.8b2 spent three rounds on (the 'K deltas per PUT' tests, the 'no PUT while idle' test, the '7 PUTs for 9 deltas at K=3' rate regression). MEASURED: writing the pointer 20 times per trigger instead of once leaves the whole sequencer suite green. I checked the obvious realistic regression too -- moving the pointer PUT to every commit -- and it IS caught today, but for the wrong reason: it fails Invariants/CommitProtocolSimulation with 'not a chain entry: bad magic', because those fixtures still decode every key under logPrefix. That is the third decode site M4.8b1's row flags for repair; when it is repaired, the accidental protection disappears with it.
findings.failure_scenario: A future change writes the pointer on every commit 'so discovery is always fresh'. After the Invariants/hasChain fixtures learn to skip non-delta keys (which M4.8b1's row already requires), nothing fails: the commit-path PUT rate has doubled per commit rather than per trigger, in the one component whose PUT rate is the M4 cost table, and no assertion in the tree says so.
findings.remedy: Count PUTs at the pointer key by name -- a pointerKeys() beside checkpointKeys() -- and assert one per trigger in the existing K-deltas fixture.

findings.summary: checkpointKeyFor's javadoc, three lines above the method this diff adds, still says the padding matters because 'M4.9 bounds replay by taking the LAST of these' -- i.e. list-and-take-last, the mechanism ADR-0034 rejects in this same commit and AC5 forbids outright. The diff had the file open and left the contradiction standing.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.9's implementer reads LogKeys, which ChainReplay's own javadoc names as the addressing seam, and finds an instruction to take the last key of the ckpt/ prefix. This project's history records that precise shape: 'a mechanism deleted from the SPEC but left standing in the backlog, which is what actually gets built' -- the M4.0 round-3 defect this very task exists because of. The result is a LIST on the recovery path that AC5 forbids and that R15 prices at fan-out.
findings.remedy: Restate the padding reason as ordering-for-an-operator-and-for-M7-retention, and point at latestCheckpointKey()/ADR-0034 for discovery.

findings.summary: 'The pointer is per-epoch ... a fenced leader's pointer is invisible to its successor' is recorded as a pure benefit, and the half that matters to the reader is missing. The successor is exactly the process that needs the predecessor's checkpoint: at takeover its own epoch has no pointer, so newestCheckpoint(store, prefix, ownEpoch) returns empty and M4.9 replays the whole ancestry. Neither the ADR nor the javadoc says which epoch a recovering leader must pass, nor that finding 'the newest checkpoint of the CHAIN' costs one stat per ancestor epoch walked. The bound still holds (constant per epoch, and the ancestry walk is bounded by firstInheritableAncestor rather than by checkpoint count), but it is a request-count consequence of the decision and the Consequences section is where it belongs.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.9 calls newestCheckpoint with the epoch it just acquired, gets empty on every takeover, and replays the whole term -- the mechanism built here doing nothing at all, with every test green because no test covers an epoch other than 1 (see M4.8c-R1b).
findings.remedy: One sentence in Consequences naming the ancestor epoch as the argument at recovery, and the per-epoch (never per-checkpoint) stat cost of the walk.

findings.summary: Two gaps in the recorded reasoning around the doubled PUT. (a) The failure-path claim -- 'a failed pointer write retries the whole checkpoint ... the seq-keyed putIfAbsent loses harmlessly' -- is TRUE by code reading (written stays false, dirty stays set, deltasSinceCheckpoint resets in the finally, and the retry converges whether or not the sequence advanced), but no test can exercise it: RecordingBinStore's injectors, failNextCheckpointPut and failEveryCheckpointPutUnchecked, are both scoped to keys ending '.ckpt', so a failure can never be armed at the pointer PUT. Its consequence is also unstated -- after a failed pointer write the pointer lags the newest .ckpt by up to one trigger, so M4.9's 'at most K deltas' is really at most about 2K. (b) Alternatives considered does not include the cheapest option: the pointer INSTEAD OF the seq-keyed object. Since the pointer carries the same bytes, the ADR's own Consequences concede the seq-keyed checkpoints are 'unread by discovery', so the alternative that keeps the budget at ONE PUT rather than doubling it is the one not weighed.
findings.failure_scenario: (a) A later change reorders the two PUTs, or clears `dirty` between them, and the convergence argument silently stops holding with no test able to see it -- the writer wedges or the pointer stays permanently behind. (b) A cost review reads the ADR, sees two PUTs justified against one, and never learns that one was available; the M4 SPEC's cost line ('Checkpoints cost one PUT per K deltas or T seconds') is now superseded only inside the ADR.
findings.remedy: Scope the injector by key rather than by suffix so the pointer PUT can be failed, state the one-trigger staleness bound, and record the pointer-only option with the reason for keeping the history (M7 retention, operator readability).
